utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. McCloskey, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Yes, just a brief preliminary. Yesterday we put in an intercept from February 1993 through Mr. Butler. It was admitted as P02192. We noticed that the first page of that, that showed the date, was not uploaded into e-court. We have now done that. If that is all right with the Chamber, of course, and we would ask that we be able to replace that in e-court. And also, it -- the doc ID is 02020586 and we have been able to do the redaction of it, as the Court wanted, so that we only see the relevant intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, is this now the full, new document, as you wish it to be admitted, which appears under this doc ID?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what was there plus now the information about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then leave is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although Madam Registrar will still verify if we have everything now but leave is granted and Madam Registrar is instructed to replace the existing exhibit in e-court by the new one known under the doc ID you just mentioned, Mr. McCloskey. And then that new replacement is the admitted evidence. Any other matter? If not, then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom? And meanwhile I'll use the time. Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber wanted to verify what can still be expected from the Prosecution in terms of upcoming bar table and Rule 92 bis and quater filings. If we have understood everything well, the Sarajevo and Srebrenica bar table motions will be filed in September still. Then, there appears to be one miscellaneous bar table motion to be filed in October and lastly it seems that there are Rule 92 bis filings outstanding for eight witnesses, namely RM096, RM098, RM182, RM183, RM184, RM378, RM379, and RM509. The Chamber expects that these motions are filed by the end of September. The Prosecution is requested to inform the Chamber, within 24 hours, whether any of the above is incorrect or not achievable or whether there are any other expected filings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. McCloskey will now have a few more questions for you in his re-examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 17520, this is a document that you were shown on cross-examination. And Mr. Butler there's a binder in front of you. There's a series of about four or five documents that I will be asking you about. The Defence has seen them and if you can take a look at those, some of them are multi-pages that you may need to review. Basically, what we are doing is -- there is a reference, as you can see, in looking at this letter from General Mladic to General Janvier of 12 June 1995, and in that second line, General Mladic references -- he -- reference our agreement of 4 June, and the Trial Chamber has asked us to look into any possible agreement. So, given this assignment from the Trial Chamber, this was passed on to Ms. Bretell who provided us with some documents and I'd like to ask you about them and get some on real time analysis, if possible, and if you need more time, let us know. But I think, if we study this briefly, we'll see that the subject matter of this letter references, among other things, the logistic needs of the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde and Sarajevo, and mentions that there's an agreement and -- and approve the transport of the most urgent supplies. There's a recommendation that it go through the FRY, that it also talks about in the next paragraph down, release four members of the RS army before your convoys start, and then finally it says we could be -- we could precise the timings and routes for these convoys. So that's the subject matter, and let me go to the first document that Ms. Bretell came up with in an attempt to answer or at least shed some light on these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can tell us -- we do not have a written agreement that is referred to but if we could go to 65 ter 17697, and this is the cover letter, we can see, and if we could now go to page 1 in the English, the original document was apparently in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is page 2 in e-court. No, let me see. You said page 1 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It should be page 1 in the B/C/S as well. And if we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can see that these -- if you can take a brief look at this, it appears to be some sort of accounting of the meeting between Janvier and General Mladic on 4 June which was -- we saw the date of that letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The B/C/S can't be the right page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem, apparently, is caused by the fact that the original French is preceded by one cover letter in English and therefore, what is in French, page 2 in e-court, is in English page 1 in e-court because there was no need to translate the cover letter which was already in English. It's a bit confusing but we are there and I think this also explains why page 1 in B/C/S is the cover letter, translation in B/C/S on page 2 is the first page of the proper text. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we -- in looking at this briefly, Mr. Butler, can you just tell roughly what you think this is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They appear to be minute notes of a meeting between General Janvier and General Mladic on this date. It looks like, from the part that I've got so far, they are discussing a very critical point in time in June of 1995 where the VRS has taken a number of UN peacekeepers hostage, NATO forces are conducting bombing operations, you have the VRS withdrawing heavy equipment out of UN monitored facilities around Sarajevo, and essentially, General Janvier is warning General Mladic that at the rate things are going, events are rapidly spinning out of control, which could cause, like everything else in combat, I mean, you know, unintended consequences and escalations. So, I mean, that's what I've got for you with reading General Janvier's positions and I'm reading General Mladic's various positions on these now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we did not see any reference to an agreement under the arguments of the force commander section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we go to General Mladic's position, it should be 4 in the English. And if we could then go through to -- my note shows that it's B/C/S page 4 and now English page 6 of what is noted down as General Mladic's positions. Can we turn the page in both to go into the next page in both? And now let's go to the next -- the next page. I'm interested in paragraph 2.3, the attitude of the Bosnian Serbs regarding the problem of the enclaves. And we can see here that we're getting into a -- the topic of the enclaves. And at the last paragraph, the -- at the bottom, it may be the next paragraph in the B/C/S, General Janvier notes that General Mladic said he was ready to allow the replenishing, as proposed, transiting the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under the condition that the latter agrees. He gave precise information on meeting points in each of the eastern enclaves in order to carry out the replenishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you connect, in any way, this statement with the letter that we saw previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe that this is the genesis of what they are talking about in that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we don't see any reference to an agreement, but in this -- if this paragraph is correct that General Mladic is allow -- is ready to allow the replenishing of the enclaves as proposed, would that be something that, in your view, that UNPROFOR in this context would agree to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, certainly UNPROFOR was saying that there, you know, in General Janvier's part, they were noting the fact that the situation with the UNPROFOR forces in the enclaves is becoming critical with respect to fuel and other -- and food and other supplies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17697 receives number P2196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. The last portion we looked at, Mr. McCloskey, was page 6 in English. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering the other document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart also informed me I need to tender 65 ter 17520, that apparently didn't get tendered during cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the one we looked at previously. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17520 receives number P2197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to P00345? These are excerpts of the Mladic diaries. If we could have page 166 in the English and B/C/S page 168? And we can now see that this is dated 4 June 1995 at 1230 hours and makes reference to a meeting with General Janvier. Could we go to the next page, which should be 167 in the English, 169 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And under the section that says General Janvier emphasised the following issues and does -- do these issues, and I point out number 2, supplies to the enclaves, comport with these other documents that suggest issues under discussion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, again this appears to be General Mladic's contemporaneous notes on the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: See any reference to anything that could be viewed as an agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, it's 65 ter 17700. And I'm sorry I don't have a B/C/S translation of this particular document but we'll get one. And can we go to the next page in the English? And we can see that this is a similar -- similar notes as the last one of a meeting between Janvier and Mladic, this one dated 17 June. And if you could briefly look at those first couple of pages. Let's go slowly to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see here specific demands by the force commander and under 23, it's entitled, "The delivery of new supplies to the soldiers in the enclaves." And we can see in that second paragraph that, with the approval of the authorities of Belgrade, the delivery of new supplies will be done through the territory of the FRY. It's imperative that this delivery, which was postponed several times, leave on Monday morning, 19 June, for the enclaves in the east. Then it says it would be -- have a disastrous effect if it didn't make it. Does this -- can you connect this to the last couple of documents we have been looking at, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Again, the high level of activity between General Mladic and General Janvier, negotiating over the issue of getting, for at least for the UNPROFOR people, getting food, fuel and other material to those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page, which is conclusion of the force commander, positions of General Mladic. First a skim. And if we could go to the next page now, now page 5 and Ms. Bretell has pointed our attention to paragraph 43. We can see that for ourselves. Now let's go to the next page, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And looking at that second paragraph, under the concession of General Mladic, we can see that it's again talking about the delivery of new supplies to the UN troops in the enclaves, food and fuel, the subject matter. We see that General Mladic was concerned about the black market, blatant abuses, then lastly we see, in this respect, the convoys of 19 June would be a test. So this document, dated June 17th, is this reference to the 19 June convoys related to this other suggestions about convoys that we have been looking at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it appears to be that they are going to set up -- they have had previous movements that have been blocked. They are going to try one more time on the 19th with again both sides trying to facilitate the activity. In this particular context General Mladic is saying we are going to inspect the convoy and if we turn it around because there is contraband items on it, the hit would be on the UN, not on his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'd offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I may be mistaken but I'm not sure about the source of the document. I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a -- it's a UN document, it's like the other ones. They were notes that we received from the UN regarding Janvier's meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, from the cover page, it seems that it is sent from Akashi in Zagreb to Annan in New York 20th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see in e-court now. I didn't see it when it was shown to us. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the original is in French as well. Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 17700 receives number P2198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The suggestion is MFI pending B/C/S translation. To be consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're right. I should have thought about that. Madam Registrar, it's not admitted, it's marked for identification pending translation into B/C/S. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. The last one of these notes 65 ter 19542, another document provided to us from Ms. Bretell. And we can see that this is something called an outgoing code cable to Mr. Annan from Mr. Akashi dated 20 June. We can review that first page briefly and then go into the second page, should be the second page in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we get to paragraph 5, it says problems with convoys, both logistic resupply and UNHCR continue in many parts of the UNPROFOR AOR. The 56 truck convoy, bound for the eastern enclaves, arrived in Belgrade yesterday. Of course, that would have been the 19th. Does this suggest to you, Mr. Butler, that this has anything to do with the previous document and the reference to the test on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then it says, however, the BSA has cut the number of trucks from 56 to 23, has cut the amount of food by 50 per cent, and the amount of fuel by 70 per cent, has rejected the passage of two ambulances needed for the UN troops. And we can read the rest of that. Preventing any troop rotation. What do you -- how does this fit into your analysis and this continuing -- both the precise analysis you've been doing for these documents and your overall analysis about the restriction of the enclaves and any possible relation to directive 7?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, at least with respect to UNPROFOR, this particular document in paragraph 5 of the report, clearly reflects the fact that the VRS is continuing a pattern of not allowing the UNPROFOR forces in the enclaves to be properly resupplied or to, essentially, bring their manpower back up to the strength that it was because they are not -- they want everyone who goes into the enclaves to come back out again. So this is clearly, you know, the MO that is listed here is clearly consistent with what we would see in the previous months, March, April, May, you know, getting to this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you have any opinion regarding whether or not General Mladic would have been aware of this 50 per cent reduction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that the convoy clearances, as demonstrated in other exhibits, went to the Main Staff and received the attention of the highest members of the Main Staff, it's unlikely that General Mladic would not be aware about this, particularly in this case, given his direct involvement with General Janvier in the earlier documents, setting up this convoy or this series of convoys on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next page. We can see that briefly. And then now let's go to the page after that. Now, looking at this big chart that appears to be connected to this -- these notes, we see Gorazde, Zepa, Srebrenica, and then BSA allowance for each one of those. It goes from nine containers with food and water to four containers with food and two with water. I won't go through all of this. Does this appear to be related to the paragraph we just looked at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Butler, if you could keep this document in front of you, I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19542 receives number P2199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to P01420? And this is a document that's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see it's from the Main Staff and the second page is -- it's in the name of Colonel Miletic dated 18 June, and Mr. Butler, if you could take a look at 1, 2, and 3. If we can see that these are three convoys that, from the first paragraph, we wish to inform you that we have approved the movement of the UNPROFOR convoy from Zagreb via Belgrade to the enclaves as follows. And perhaps we could replace the B/C/S with this chart that we just had up on the board so everyone can make a comparison. Could you see if those three convoys are related, in any way, to the three convoys on that chart? As with most such documents we can see for ourselves, the first one was for Zepa, the second one was for Gorazde, and the third one was for Srebrenica but do the amounts in it -- are they similar, or the same, to the ones noted in the UN form? And I take it CUM is cubic metres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, sir. Yes, sir. At least with respect to fuel it looks consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, it is exactly now that you used double the time you indicated yesterday. You said you would need 15 minutes, you've now used 30 minutes. Could you please stick to your time limits and be more precise in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll be happy to hear, Mr. President, that's -- I'm finished. That was the last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the last question. Then you made it in 200 per cent of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Important to answer your question. I'm sorry I couldn't have done it shorter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic I do understand that I have to address to you ask whether there is any need for further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think just shortly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Butler, my name is Branko Lukic. Due to medical or rather health reasons, my colleague Mr. Ivetic could not be here today so I will have a few questions to put to you in his stead. You told us about P2196, which is actually a letter or, rather, the minutes of the meeting between General Janvier and General Mladic which took place on 4 June 1995. Earlier today in the transcript you mentioned or rather you described the times, there were hostages, NATO was bombarding the positions of the VRS, and the Serbs were withdrawing weapons from the place where they were supposed to be under control. In your analysis, did you see or did you notice that at that time the Muslims also withdrew weapons from the points where they were supposed to be under control, in Sarajevo? Did you notice that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, given the context of my focus was on Srebrenica, I did not pay much attention to issues related to Sarajevo, so I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] You also spoke about convoys earlier today, humanitarian convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up in e-court 1D1024. I need the following page in B/C/S, and I believe that the corresponding page in English will also be page 2. Or, rather, this is -- the only translation we have. Only the first page has been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your work were you aware of the existence of the state committee on cooperation with the United Nations and international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I was. I believe I talked about it earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After the month of March 1995, did you observe or did you establish who was it who made decisions on the passage of those convoys? Was it still the VRS or was it somebody else?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I indicated in my earlier testimony, this particular committee was in charge of dealing with issues of approving the UNHCR and other international organisation convoys but as I also again indicated, that ultimately, the VRS, because they were the armed force on the ground and controlling the roads, ultimately it was their determination whether these convoys would pass or not because they are the ones who had to clear them through. So, again, the decision may have been made by the political organs, but given the fact that there was a conflict going on, whether or not a convoy could proceed ultimately was at the discretion of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see an instance in which the VRS acted contrary to the decision of political bodies in this particular sense, i.e. when it came to the passage of convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that I looked at reflect the fact that the -- not that they are acting contrary but they are trying to make sure that the political bodies understand that these things do have to be coordinated with them before they can allow these convoys to travel through the territory of the -- of where the conflict was going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who had the last say in all that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, my view is that the army had the final say because regardless of whether the political authorities would grant clearance to the convoy or not, it was the army's responsibility, if for no other reason for safety and security of the convoy people, to decide to allow them to go through. If there was fighting going on or something of that nature, clearly the army wouldn't let them through. So again in that context, the army had the final say because they physically were on the ground and controlling the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say that the army wouldn't allow passage and would not give clearance to a convoy because of the ongoing fighting. Are you saying that political body gave clearance to a convoy but the VRS decided to oppose that decision and not allow the passage of that particular convoy due to the ongoing fighting? Do you have an example to share with us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I was just using it as an example to your question as to who had the final say on whether a convoy would transit through and of using that as an example to illustrate why I believed that the VRS had the final say, because ultimately they controlled the road network and they controlled the check-points into the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The last part of my question was about an example you may be able to share with us. Are you aware of any such example? Is there an example which you can share with us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I have not seen a VRS document which has gone back to the political organs saying that they denied access of a convoy going through with respect to at least Srebrenica. They may have delayed it or things of that nature, but I've not seen one that I recall where they basically turned around and said we flat out deny access, we don't care what you've said about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Butler, it was all we had for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. This, then, concludes the testimony of you, Mr. Butler, but before we continue, we don't need the witness for tendering any of the reports and decisions on admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I wouldn't think so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Butler, I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for staying quite a while in The Hague, and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home, although perhaps a little bit later than you expected, a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, anything left to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler's reports, which I have a list of. I can give the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we start with hearing from the Defence whether there are overall objections or still --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, all our objections still stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And since you ruled that our objections go to the weight attributed to the reports - there are three reports - we would maintain objections to the remaining two reports and I could address that. If you allow me, I would just read what Mr. Ivetic left for me to be read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we then take them one by one? Is that report-specific, to say so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then, Mr. McCloskey, if you introduce the first one and then we will go through them one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. The first would be 04624, the Corps Responsibility Report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Regarding this one, you ruled that our objections go to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The second one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 04625, the Brigade Command Responsibility Report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Same situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same situation. Next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 04626, the Srebrenica Military Narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We do object to this one. And if you want me, I can read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you have anything to --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you would like to bring to our attention before we decide, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This one and the one marked as 04627 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- Srebrenica Trial Narrative Revised, we would give the following additional reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we are dealing now with both 04626 and 04627.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Srebrenica trial narratives are based on witness testimonies from the Krstic case and the witness's interpretation of documents. Our objections makes moot the grounds. Mere interpretation of documents are not an appropriate expertise as it invades on the role of the Chamber to interpret documents. In the Milutinovic and in the Djordjevic cases, the Chamber decided to treat Mr. Phil Coo and the Defence witness as experts because their only declined -- sorry, the Chamber declined to treat Phil Coo and the Defence witness as experts because they only interpreted documents. We believe the Srebrenica trial narratives are of the same type and therefore should not be allowed. For example, Milutinovic decision on Prosecution motion for admission of evidence in connection of Philip Coo from 23 March 2007, and in Djordjevic case, decision on Prosecution notice re Defence expert witnesses from 24 March 2010. These reports rely on and recite evidence from the Krstic case that has not been led in this case and which does not take into account the state of evidence which was presented in this case. The witness testified in the cross that 74 footnotes in the revised Srebrenica narrative recite evidence of witnesses in the Krstic case. It's on transcript page 16575 to 16576. We submit it is not within the proper expertise of the witness to recite what witnesses said in other cases. So, for both of those reasons, we object to the inclusion of the two Srebrenica trial narratives into evidence. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have reviewed the narratives and counted that Mr. Butler has cited information or testimony of 31 witnesses, and of those 31 witnesses, there is a total of 12 of those witnesses that are not in evidence in this case or not been presented as 92 bis or quater in this case, so that gets us to fundamentally 12 witnesses. Six of those witnesses are Bosnian Muslim civilians who identify neighbours of theirs that Mr. Butler was able to tie to the Bratunac Brigade roster. So you have a witness that sees a Serb neighbour, Mr. Butler takes that and tells us in his narrative that that person is -- was in the Bratunac Brigade. Then of the remaining six, he speaks briefly about something Ljubisa Borovcanin said, Dragomir Vasic said, and Milos Stupar said at -- about a 15 July meeting that you may recall that occurred at the Zvornik Brigade, and that information comes in through other witnesses and none of those three witnesses are we relying on for the truth of the matter. It helps put the -- as Mr. Butler said on the stand and as he says in his report, it helps put that meeting in context. And for 10, 11 and 12, one is a Dutch soldier that talks about Muslim prisoners being brought from Potocari to the Vuk Karadzic school, which is evidence that comes in in this case through another Dutch soldier. 11 was a comment from Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans where he -- Mr. Butler passes on his remark that at the third meeting, Mladic said that men between 16 to 60 would be screened. That evidence, you may recall, came in through Boering. We are certainly not relying on that comment from Mr. Karremans in any way. Again puts Mr. Butler's narrative in context. And the 12th person was a survivor of the Orahovac execution and talks about that and his experience at the Vuk Karadzic school which is -- we are not relying on and that all of that evidence comes in through other Orahovac survivors. So I don't think it's a problem. It's not violating 92 bis or 92 quater. The Court will have the ability to take any of these references and give it whatever weight it deems necessary. So that would be my response to that, in particular, challenge by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all as far as tendering is concerned, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, there were annexes to the narratives which I'm sure will be the subject of the objections as well. If I could go through those just briefly, the 65 ters of those annexes. The annex A to the Drina Corps command report, 04629. Annex B to the Zvornik Brigade structure, 04630. Annex C, the Bratunac Brigade structure, 04631. Annex D, the police structure in the Drina Corps, 04632. Annex E Main Staff structure, 04633. And then a report entitled, "Chapter 8, analytical addendum to the Srebrenica narrative, revised," 04634. And a report entitled, "VRS Main Staff Command Responsibility Report," 05601. And I had missed the narrative that was revised, which was 04627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that was addressed already together with 04626, I think. Mr. Lukic, anything to add in relation to these annexes and to the documents just listed by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nothing to be added, just that we object and one of these is not in this category, it's 05601, Main Staff report, since it was -- has already been ruled that the objections to this one go to the weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have all the arguments in favour and objecting to admission. We have them on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there are a few which the Chamber could perhaps already decide on immediately, the Chamber would prefer that Madam Registrar provides MFI numbers, perhaps in a written document, making a list and we'll then decide on admission. Madam Registrar, if that -- could you -- you don't have to read it now. If you prepare it -- -

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then we'll deal with it once a decision will be taken. Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness, General Milovanovic, is a witness who the Chamber might consider it appropriate to give him advice of the rights he has under Rule 90(E), so I would ask the Chamber to consider that over the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider that over the break. We'll take the break and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If -- is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness, which we do understand is Mr. Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution calls General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milovanovic. Before you give evidence, the rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovanovic. Please be seated. Mr. Milovanovic, before we -- the Prosecution will start its examination, I'd like to draw your attention to the following. Under the rules of this Tribunal, a witness, that would be you in this case, may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate that witness, that is that would incriminate yourself. We, then, however, we could compel you to answer that question, although an answer compelled in this way could not be used against you in any way. I just want you to be aware that you have the opportunity to object to making such a statement, which might incriminate yourself. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I add to this that if you are compelled to answer, and if -- and that answer cannot be used against you apart from the situation where you're not telling us the truth. So such a statement could be used as evidence if there would be reasons to prosecute you for false testimony. Mr. Milovanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Groome. Mr. Groome is counsel for the Prosecution. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to state your full name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it true that you are appearing here today pursuant to a subpoena issued by this Chamber on 24 July 2013 and served on you in Banja Luka several weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, is there any agreement of immunity between you and the ICTY Prosecutor? In other words, is there or has there ever been any agreement between you and the Prosecution that if you provided information related to its investigations and prosecutions, that you yourself would not be investigated or indicted?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have never reached any agreement with anybody from this Tribunal. The only thing that happened was that I was interviewed on 27th of March, 2001, by your military expert, General Richard Butler who has just left the courtroom. That interview was about helping the Tribunal to see the other side of the coin, as it were. I.e. how could military experts from the VRS provide their statements before this Tribunal? That interview was recorded on seven pages, which I handed over to the OTP of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was anything ever said to you which you implicitly understood as a promise that you would not be indicted?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to provide evidence on a number of issues of importance in this trial. In order to do this in a way that the Chamber can best understand your evidence, it is important that we do it in an organised way. I would like to begin my questions to you this morning by asking you some questions about your background. Can you tell us the year and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on 21st November 1943 in Laminci village in the municipality of Gradiska, Republika Srpska, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 26000 be brought to our screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that is being brought to our screens, can I ask you what year did you enter military service?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The date when I entered the JNA was the 27th of July, 1961. That was when I completed my education for non-commissioned officers. I started that education on the 30th of August, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what year did you retire from military service?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was pensioned off on the 31st of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, if I can direct your attention to the screen before you, you have had a lengthy professional career. While it is important that the Chamber is aware of the positions you held, it is not necessary that we discuss it in any great detail at this moment. After you arrived in The Hague, were you asked to review a summary of your professional assignments?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And is that what we see on our screens now before us?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we go to the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And, General, if I can draw your attention to the end of the document. Upon reviewing this document, did you wish to amend it by adding two additional pieces of information?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When it says career in the Army Republika Srpska and where it says chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, I would like to add to that that I was also the deputy commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. And the second thing that I wanted to add was that I served as the Minister of Defence in the government of Republika Srpska from the 18th of January, 1998, to the day when I was pensioned off, on the 31st of March, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, with those amendments the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 26000 into evidence as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26000 receives number P2211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2211 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, are you willing to answer any additional questions regarding your professional career that either the Chamber or the Defence may have for you?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, can you tell us how long have you known General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I met General Mladic in April 1981. We first met in the Titov Veles garrison where he had arrived to inspect the unit where I served as the chief of the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, he was the commander of the Army of Republika Srpska and you were his deputy. Can you describe in a summary way his command style as well as yours? I'm not asking you to tell us about any specific events at this moment, but to simply summarise, in a sentence or two, your respective command styles.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: His command style will be best explained if I quote his own words from those times. On one occasion, I asked him, "Why did you choose me to be your deputy?" And he told me, "I am quick tempered, and you are somewhat slower and as a tank man you know that that's the best way to drive." And one of his statements, at meetings or when we were eye to eye, he told me that the two of us were two bodies and one soul.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can you please describe your relationship with General Mladic during your tenure as his Chief of Staff and deputy commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war broke out, we were friends. We were comrades. We sometimes agreed to disagree in professional matters. However, during the war, our relationship was that of a very strict military subordination, a relationship between a subordinate and superior. Before the war we were not on first-term basis, and as the war -- or rather, we were on first-term basis before -- on the first-name basis before the war, and then I started, out of respect, addressing him in a more respectful plural form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I want to now turn your attention to the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska and I want to ask you to explain to the Judges the events leading to the establishments of the VRS and your role in those events. Can I draw your attention to February of 1992, in particular the JNA's withdrawal of its forces from Macedonia? Can you tell us what, if any, role you had in that event?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1992, and you say that it was in February, at that time, the JNA was withdrawing from Macedonia after an agreement had been reached to that effect. We are talking about a 3rd Army. And the troops were being deployed in the territory of Serbia, Kosovo, and some of them in Montenegro. I was tasked with supervising the withdrawal of the combat part of the JNA, i.e. personnel, weapons, and ammunition, and I was supposed to deploy them across the aforementioned areas. There was just one condition, i.e. I received just one order, that during the withdrawal, not a single bullet could be fired on the Macedonian people. We did everything very efficiently, owing to the Macedonian authorities, which were committed not to allow any provocations, ill treatment of members of the JNA, something that was seen previously in Slovenia, Croatia, and in the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The process was completed on the 9th of March, 1992. We started withdrawing on the 3rd of March from Skopje to Nis, and on the 9th of March the logistics part of the 3rd Army eventually withdrew from Macedonia and completed the whole withdrawal process.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, where were you stationed between March and the 11th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Nis garrison, in the command of the 3rd Army. I was the chief of operations and education body, and I was the acting chief of the army command because General Vukovic was supposed to arrive from Banja Luka in order to become the chief of the army. Vukovic arrived in Nis on the 20th of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'm not sure that we need all that much detail in that particular aspect. Could I draw your attention now to the 8th of May, 1992? Did you receive an order from the president -- Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on that day?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received two decrees on that day, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you tell us what each one was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to one of the decrees, I was reassigned from the Nis garrison to the Sarajevo garrison, where I was to serve in the command of the 2nd Army District as the chief of the operations and education body, and it said on that -- in that decree that General Mladic was also assigned from Knin to Sarajevo to become the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District. And the second decree, I don't know which was one was the first and which one was the second, according to the second decree from the Presidency of the SFRY, I was promoted to the rank of Major General. On that same piece of paper, it stated that General Ratko Mladic was also promoted to the rank of Lieutenant General.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, when you received this order, did you have an understanding of any particular task you were to undertake when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to that first decree, I believe that on the following day, I called General Mladic and I asked him if he knew anything more about that decree and about that order, because our names were on the same piece of paper. He told me, and you have to be aware that that was on the 8th of May, when the whole situation surrounding Dobrovoljacka Street was completed, i.e. when the command of the 2nd Army District was withdrawn from Sarajevo. General Mladic told me that General Kukanjac, commander of the 2nd Army District, would probably be removed from his position as well as his Chief of Staff, General Stankovic, I believe that his name was but I don't know. He also told me that he would possibly become the commander of the military district in which case I would become the Chief of Staff of the 2nd Military District. In practical terms, that meant that the second decree that we received promoted us one step further in the command of the 2nd Military District. The second decree was shown to me in Belgrade on the 11th of May, because General Mladic and I had agreed to meet in Belgrade in the General Staff of the JNA building at 7.00 on the 11th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us when it was that you agreed with General Mladic to meet him on 11 May? When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was on the 9th of May, when I called him. The day after I received my first decree. When I wanted him to give me more detail. I arrived on the 11th of May at 7.00 but General Mladic was not there. The chief of the personnel of the Yugoslav General Staff received me. He was General Vojko Krstic, I believe. He then verbally communicated to me the contents of the second decree about the vertical promotion in the command of the Sarajevo Military District, and I was not very happy and I told him, and I asked him how come that Mladic and I, and some other people who had received those orders, were being transferred to Sarajevo knowing that the 2nd Military District didn't exist? I was told then that the JNA was tasked with withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina before the 19th of May, 1992. That was to be within the next eight days. The way I saw it was that the JNA was disappearing from Bosnia-Herzegovina and I really didn't understand why we should be in Sarajevo if the command was no longer in Sarajevo and actually it no longer existed. I was told that General Mladic would be able to explain. I asked him to put me through to General Mladic. I was put through to General Mladic. The General was somewhere in Herzegovina at the time. He told me this: Go to Batajnica. Go to the airport. A helicopter is waiting for you there. Get on board and wherever the pilot stops, that's where you should be. That's where you should be waiting for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just to ensure that it's not becoming confused, who was it that told you that the JNA would be withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Gojko Krstic. And that same evening, that was confirmed to me by General Mladic himself, once we met.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So did you in fact meet with General Mladic in Batajnica on the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. General Mladic ordered me to go to Batajnica because there was a helicopter waiting for me there and that helicopter took me to Crna Rijeka, near Han Pijesak. As for my meeting with General Mladic, I met him a few hours later when he arrived from Herzegovina. That was sometime after 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us who else, if anyone, was present during this meeting with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was waiting for General Mladic near the helicopter. I don't think that anybody else was present. We started walking towards a prefabricated building that was closest to the place where the helicopter landed. It was some 50 metres away. And it took us about 45 minutes to walk the distance, if not more. And while we were walking, Mladic told me about the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he put me in the picture, he told me more or less what we were to expect. We walked into that prefabricated buildings and in one of the rooms there, there were some other people, some ten people. So all in all, there were about a dozen of us there, four generals, Mladic, Djukic, Gvero, and myself, and eight or rather seven lieutenant-colonels, colonels and one captain. There was a dozen of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before we get to the substance of this meeting, the record records you as saying that Mladic told you: More or less what you were to expect, what we were to expect. Can I ask you to give us a bit more detail on what Mladic told you was to be expected?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when we greeted each other I asked him, "And now what?" And then he told me that the war in Bosnia was inevitable, that there were combat operations going on around Sarajevo, primarily around Sarajevo and in some other municipalities of the future Republika Srpska, that armed incidents had already started, mostly on the line separating the members of the Muslim and Croat coalition on the one hand and members of the JNA on the other. The skirmishes started already on the 22nd of April when some mortars opened fire on the Serbian settlements in Sarajevo and the fire was opened from a brewery. And then on the bank holiday on the 1st of May there were some attacks on the command of the 2nd Military District, on the military hospital, on the JNA hall, and a few barracks, which accommodated cadets of JNA military academies. I don't know which barracks existed in Sarajevo at that time -- at the time, by inter alia military cadets were attacked in Pazarici shooting round. General Mladic's conclusion was that the war is inevitable in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that it would follow the same scenario as in Croatia when the war broke out between the Croats and the Serbs. Up to that time, Muslims --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can I ask you now to tell us, or recount for us, what occurred during the meeting that General Mladic had with yourself and these other 12 people?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the room where we were assembled, General Mladic first told us what we had discussed en route from the helicopter to the building, the conversation he and I had. He said that the war was imminent in all likelihood, and that, since the JNA was prematurely withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina because previously it had been agreed that the JNA would remain in BiH for the next five years, until 1997, in order to protect the interests of all three majority peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina, acting as a buffer zone, which is something it had done previously in Croatia and Slovenia. Since the JNA had to withdraw that protection that was to be accorded to the Serb people was no longer and that it was the position of the BiH leadership, Serb leadership, decided to establish the army of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The next day, on the 12th of May, a decision was supposed to be made during an assembly session of the Serbian people to be held in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now turn your attention to that assembly session? Did you attend that session?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall what you did that day, the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. However, it might be good if I told you what we did during the night between the 11th and the 12th of May, just before the assembly session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, please do that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That evening, we only supposed that General Mladic was going to be appointed commander of the Main Staff by the assembly. We knew that the Main Staff had no documents pertaining to its doctrine in wartime, should the assembly decide in favour of the war option, which is what indeed happened the next day. Those of us as peers acting together with General Mladic as the first among equals, we discussed what was to be done once the decision is in place. Some 21 tasks became obvious. We formulated them and later on, actually, they were not tasks but conclusions, and later on, I grouped them into some ten guidelines, in terms of the future Republika Srpska Army doctrine. It started with us having to rely, or make use of, all what remained after JNA's withdrawal, so as to use it as the basis to create the new armed forces of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then, the conclusions and discussions further developed such issues as armaments, unifying the armed forces, et cetera. And according to General Mladic's words, the then-party in power, SDS, had distributed weapons to the Serb military conscripts and according to Mr. Mladic's -- General Mladic's words, by that time we have already had between 85 and 90.000 people who were armed and who had to be made a part of the structure. We also discussed the issue of paramilitaries, of which there were many in the territory of what today is Republika Srpska and at the time was the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was agreed that the commanders, dukes or bosses of those paramilitary forces be assembled, someone to have a talk with them, so that they would be asked to place themselves under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska. Whoever accepted that was welcome. Those who refused had to leave the territory of Republika Srpska as agreed. Those who opposed it were supposed to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you a few specific questions about that answer that you've just given us? Did you consider that the group that had been gathered together for this meeting, did you consider that group to be the early formation of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have to dwell on it too long. During our walk from the helicopter to the building, I told General Mladic the following: I had thought that I was supposed to be appointed commander of the Herzegovina corps since General Perisic was withdrawing from the JNA and I told General Mladic that I had sufficient time to arrive in Bileca by helicopter but he said: You are not going anywhere, you are staying here. If the decision is put in place tomorrow you will be the chief of the Main Staff and my deputy. So by that point, it was all clear to me. During the session, as you rightly noted, it was so decided and I did see it as the nucleus of the Main Staff and of the future Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to ask you one more question about your recounting of this meeting. You said that there was an assessment that there were 90.000 armed people. Was that an assessment of the number of armed people that would be available for the VRS army or was that an assessment of all people of all ethnicities who had arms in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not think about the ethnic makeup but what I learned was that the 85.000 to 90.000 armed men were put inside TO brigades in the municipalities around the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some of the municipalities deeper inside the territories also formed their own TO brigades. Their staffing strength and manning levels were very diverse depending on the ethnic makeup and number of population in each of the municipalities. The figure varied from a few hundred to a few thousand armed men who, by that time, were still not under any kind of unified command. The party in power had established Crisis Staffs in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can just be a bit more specific in my question: That 90.000, did that figure, was that the assessment of the armed men that were available to be formed into an Army of Republika Srpska? Is that what that figure referred to?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic said this, more or less: Now we have between 85 and 90.000 men who are armed. I don't know where he received that information from but we obviously saw it as relevant. He also said that they were supposed to be placed inside military units, given structure, and grouped into different corps. So in addition to the remnants of the JNA, it was another contingent or another element that we relied on or counted on when we were structuring the army. It was also the most important, the most significant, component.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now go to my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to avoid any misunderstanding, the 85 to 90.000 men, armed men, were men to be recruited for what would become the VRS; is that what you're referring to? Or at least available to be recruited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither, because the decree on general mobilisation in the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina followed only ten days later. It was simply a potential that could be absorbed into the structure of the newly created armed forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers my question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now return my earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just from my understanding does this number include those who have previously served for the JNA? In the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Those who had served with the JNA were included under the category of the remnants of the JNA. They were supposed to remain with the armed force after the 19th of May, once the JNA had withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now return to my earlier question about what you did on the 12th of May while the 16th Assembly session was taking place?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was the 19th session but perhaps it is not so important. At dawn, General Mladic, General Djordje Djukic, General Gvero, Colonel Tolimir, flew to Banja Luka. I was tasked to stay in Crna Rijeka and during the day, out of the 12 who had met the previous night and a number of officers from the 2nd Military District who were extracted, who withdrew on the 3rd of May together with the rest of the 2nd Army Command, I was supposed to take all those men to establish and make operational a body in charge of creating the armed force and waging the war which was imminent. In other words I was supposed to create the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Who gave that you task?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My second task was to use those officers who had fled from Sarajevo to work with them on the 21 conclusions I have mentioned. We were supposed to transform them into appropriate orders, information and notifications, that is to say to put them in written form which was mostly dealt with. My next task was to establish communication with the detached corps commands of the former JNA, to preserve their infrastructure. There were already people in place who had been corps commanders in the JNA. Thus, it was a key task, to establish direct links between the Main Staff, corps commands, logistics, the logistics base, whose infrastructure was inherited from the JNA, as well as some other parts that were supposed to be directly linked to the Main Staff. That was done before the team returned from Banja Luka. There were some other minor things also, such as providing the guards service, securing the Main Staff location, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you two questions about that last answer? Who gave you these tasks?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who else than General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you said that -- the record records you as saying that was done before they returned from Banja Luka. What was done before they returned from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: All of the things I've mentioned. So the written orders were drafted, as well as notifications, information, reports and so on and so forth. Next, communication was put in place with the subordinate commands. The security service around the Main Staff was set up. The offices and premises in the two buildings we found were distributed, in terms of who was to work where. I did not go name by name but I simply assigned offices to the commander of the Main Staff, his deputy, operations officer, command centre, and so on and so forth. Because at the time, there were only 12 of us in the Main Staff, but we expected that our staffing levels would increase once the Main Staff was fully established. I thought I would have time to do that in peacetime. But, as we were establishing communication with the subordinate commands, we began receiving combat reports. General Mladic had not warned me of this once he left, and I had to make do. It turned out that there was fighting all over Sarajevo. The Muslims were aware of JNA's withdrawal and they were attacking all things JNA, including personnel, property and equipment. So from one moment to the next, I kept receiving reports of combat. It was happening along the way and we had to deal with it. I believe we managed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, when did the team return from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was already dark by the time they gathered in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And was it on the same day as the assembly session, on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think so. Well, actually, it is, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And am I understanding your evidence correctly that before they returned, effective communications had been established with subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I began explaining about the corps commands when I was interrupted. I don't know whether you want me to continue in that vein.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt you. Yes, can you explain what tasks you completed with respect to the corps commands?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, communication was established, push-button communication was established, protected communication, with each of the corps commands. We had a command desk in the building, and we had a button for each corps command. It was sufficient for the general to press the appropriate button in order to be responded to by a colleague from the subordinate command at the corps level.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where was this push-button protected communications set up? In whose office?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There was literally a desk, rather than a specific point. It was in the office where General Mladic and I sat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when the men returned from the 12th assembly session, did you have a conversation with Colonel Gvero regarding what some people said at the assembly session and, in particular, something General Mladic said?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you: General Gvero. All of them expressed their views and impressions. It was important for me that General Mladic said something to this effect: Chief of Staff, as from this day, we are a legitimate, lawful Main Staff. I am part of the Main Staff. You are the chief of that staff and my deputy. And he repeated what he had said the previous evening. He told us who was to take up which duty out of the 12 of us. People expressed their impressions. They were discussing different deputies' remarks, and in all that, General Gvero said that following Dragan Kalinic's remarks, who was the Minister of Health in the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who asked that the Muslim people be proclaimed the enemy, the enemy side, saying that no further life together is possible with them and that we had to deal with them once and for all. Following his remarks, General Mladic reacted to it, at least according to what General Gvero told me, and later on I indeed found it in the transcript of the Assembly. It seems that General Mladic said, he actually cautioned all those present that the minister's proposal or position would amount to genocide and that it was prohibited. One could actually find it on one of the transcript pages of that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, would that be a convenient place to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is a convenient moment for a break. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is escorted in, I have to make a correction on something I said earlier today. We were discussing P2192. There was a problem with the date and a new version of P2192 was uploaded. I then said: And then that new replacement is the admitted evidence. I had overlooked that it was marked for identification. So therefore I should have said: And then the new replacement is the exhibit marked for identification, because there is still a general objection pending against the intercepts. That is hereby corrected. If there is anything to be distributed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I ask at this time, P431 be brought to our screens? It is a transcript of the 16th Assembly session held on the 12th of May. Can I ask that we go to page 34 in the original and 35 in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Milovanovic, just before the break, you said one could actually find it on the transcript pages of that session. When this transcript comes up before you, can I ask you to review it and, if you see the portion of the transcript which you believe is what Gvero was referring to, could I please ask you to read that portion?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The letters are really small. I can't see. Can the page be zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that we zoom in on the top half and then we will go to the bottom half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And see if you see the portion that you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We won't be able to see anything you point to, so if you can simply read the passage, if you do see it. Sorry it's gone from our screens now. It's being returned.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But now I've lost that part that includes genocide. Scroll up a little. I found it. It is on the screen now but I'm not supposed to touch the screen. I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "Therefore, we cannot clean, we cannot have a sieve to sift everybody but the Serbs, or for the Serbs to go through the sieve and the rest to leave. This cannot happen. I don't know what Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic are going to tell the world. This is genocide. We have to call everybody who has not been able to enter the territory of the state that we want to create their places here with us. Mr. Ostojic said it well. He noticed things very well. He saw that picture in my native village and then there is a description of how we went to that village." Should I go on reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm just asking you to identify the passage that Gvero referred to. If you've done that, then there is no need to continue reading.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in my next series of questions, I will ask you to describe your understanding of the legal structures of the VRS and the name -- and name the individuals who held particular positions. I would ask you not to volunteer too much detail at this moment. Once the Chamber has a clear overview of the structure, I will then ask you more detailed questions. So my first question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- before you do that, is it possible to see what the witness was reading in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's on -- about the middle of the page, if we can go to the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The first third, at the end of the first third of that page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So my first question about the legal structure of the VRS is: Can you tell the Chamber what the Supreme Command was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command was the political body of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in charge of warfare. It is said that war is a thing too serious for generals to run it. It has to be run by politicians and generals should only be executors. As for the Supreme Command, from 12 May, it was the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the president of the Presidency was Radovan Karadzic, the vice -- one of the vice-presidents was Biljana Plavsic, and the other was Nikola Koljevic. The president of National Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik was also a member of the Presidency, although I don't think that was really legitimate. That was the four people who politically ran the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And before the Supreme Command -- or, rather, before the Main Staff was set up, the Main Staff received its task from President Karadzic, who told him how to run the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, if you'll allow me, I want to ask some very specific questions. If I could ask you to limit your answer to the particular question just to ensure that the Chamber understands this Supreme Command. When was it formed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about the setting up of the Supreme Command on the 6th December 1992, which means it was set up in the first half of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Prior to December 1992, did Radovan Karadzic serve as the supreme commander or political commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the Supreme Command was set up, Radovan Karadzic was the supreme commander, based on the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and subsequently drafted acts on the defence and Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, which members of the Supreme Command, once it was constituted in 1992 -- in December 1992, could issue direct orders to the army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Supreme Command was established, its members were the four persons that I already mentioned, plus the prime minister of the Serbian Republic, the minister of defence, and the minister of the interior. At first, the vice-presidents or the vice prime ministers were not members of the Supreme Command and neither was General Ratko Mladic, although he should have been its members according to the act on All People's Defence. The Main Staff held it against Karadzic that Mladic was not a member, and then they included Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic as members of the Supreme Command but not General Ratko Mladic. The Main Staff insisted to no avail. They maintained that General Mladic in the Supreme Command would mean that it would be the Supreme Command of the Main Staff.
