The first session was held on the 12 December. I attended that session, and pursuant to an order of the Main Staff, I presented those objections. Karadzic told me that he could not change that, that that could not be changed, that Mladic could not be a member of the Supreme Command because, allegedly, the military was not a political body, whereas the Supreme Command was. This is how things would be done during the war. All the orders and directives and other combat documents would be issued to the Main Staff and the Army of Republika Srpska only by him as the Supreme Commander. No other members of the Supreme Command could issue orders to the army save for the persons that he appointed to act on his behalf in his absence when he was abroad, and the most often that person designated by him would be Biljana Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, just so the record is clear, when you say that -- when you refer to "him" as the Supreme Commander, are you referring to Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And also to be clear, you said that General Mladic was not a member of the Main Staff. Despite not having -- not being a member and not having a vote on its decisions, did members of the Main Staff regularly attend meetings convened by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that meeting where President Karadzic and I tried to convince each other of our respective views, he said that he would invite General Mladic or one of his assistants to all of the Supreme Command sessions depending on the topics on the agenda. If the Supreme Command was to make a decision by voting, we were not to be allowed to take part in the voting, i.e. we would be treated as observers only. That's how things were done throughout the existence of the Supreme Command and the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, before we continue, could you have a look at page 46, the first two lines of your previous question? You said and also to be clear, I think -- 46, line 22, it's for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I think we are only up, according to my LiveNote, to page 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 25 in e-court, which is 46 or 47 in LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 25 on -- it would be page 25, line 11, especially the fourth and the fifth word, also to be clear, you said that General Mladic was not a member of -- and then I would expect you to refer to the Supreme Command rather than to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify the confusion with the page numbers, in e-court, page 22 ended at line 13 and then the entire transcript started again with page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Clarified now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's been clarified. You intended to refer to not being a member of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That nevertheless members of the Main Staff being invited to meetings although not voting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this having been corrected now, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, can you give us some sense of how frequently General Mladic or other members of the Main Staff attended meetings of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you. I don't know how many times the Supreme Command met. They may have met without inviting us. But I can tell you that it was rather often that either General Mladic or I were invited, if General Mladic was not in Bosnia, or one of General Mladic's assistants would be invited. For example, on the 6th of December, I was informed about the setting up of the Supreme Command by General Djordje Djukic and Lieutenant-Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. They had been invited to a meeting in Pale and that's when Karadzic told them that the Supreme Command had been set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I now want to turn to the structure of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And while I do this, I would ask that 65 ter 26016 be brought to our screens. It's an organisational chart. I have a large copy of this in the courtroom, which General Milovanovic will be invited to point to to describe the organisation of the VRS, and I have distributed copies to both Chambers and the Defence. They may find it easier to have a version of this document in front of them as General Milovanovic is asked to explain the organisational structure of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General Milovanovic, somewhere on the desk in front of you there should be a pointer. There is no need for you to get out of your chair, hopefully. Now, my first question to you is: Do you recall being asked to review an organisational chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, Mr. Milovanovic, if possible, please remain seated because the microphone will not catch your words when you're standing, so to the extent possible, remain seated. If not possible, then please stand and then return to your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall being asked to review an organisational chart of the Main Staff and other components of the VRS by the Office of the Prosecutor in an earlier case?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 2007, between the 29th of May and the 1st of June, when I testified in the Srebrenica group case. I was given the same chart to peruse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is the -- the diagram that's next to you, which is 65 ter 26016, is that a copy of the chart that you reviewed in that earlier case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could the usher assist General Milovanovic? I think he's asking for the thing to be adjusted so he can more easily point to items. Could I ask it just be back a bit so that I can see the witness? I'm unable to see the witness. Okay. Thank you. That's good.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot move my neck horizontally which is why I asked for the chart to be closer. Yes, this is the chart which I amended. For example, in the first version some of the units were omitted. Some of the staff organs were linked erroneously to wrong bodies. This has been corrected in the meantime. I don't know what you would like to know more specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you specific questions about this chart. Now, this chart is comprised of a series of boxes indicating different organisational components of the VRS. At the top of this chart, at the centre, we see a box with General Mladic's name inside. Can I first direct you to the two boxes to the right of General Mladic's box? The first one to the left has the name of Warrant Officer Rajko Banduka. Can you tell us who he was and what was the responsibility of the warrant officer to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Warrant Officer Rajko Banduka was General Mladic's adjutant throughout the war. He received his telephone calls, he received his mail, he forwarded whatever mail needed to be forwarded to General Mladic. So he was like a personal assistant to General Mladic throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To the right of that box is a box containing two names and is entitled, "Department for Civil Affairs." Can you give us a brief summary of what was the area of responsibility of this department?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Department for Civil Affairs was subsequently set up sometime in mid-1994. The Supreme Command issued a decision that a commission should be set up at the government level and that commission would be in charge of cooperating with UNPROFOR in respect of the transport of humanitarian aid into the enclaves. Our representative, the representative of the Main Staff in that commission, was Colonel Milos Djurdjic. His assistant was Colonel Slavko Kralj. I don't know where Djurdjic was before that but I know that Slavko Kralj was a member of the 1st Krajina Corps in the command and he was in charge in liaising with foreigners, with non-governmental organisations that were involved in humanitarian aid, with UNPROFOR and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I now direct your attention to the seven boxes immediately below General Mladic's name and connected to him with a black line. These are seven sectors or components of the Main Staff. I'm going to ask you to go one by one and tell the Chamber what each sector or component was responsible for. Please pause after each sector so I can ask you some additional questions about it. I will work from left to right. The first box is entitled "staff sector" and has your name at the top. Can you summarise the areas of responsibility which came under this sector?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The staff sector. It is one of the key sectors in the Main Staff. It is in charge of combat readiness of the armed forces, the use of the armed forces, carrying out analyses of the functioning of the armed forces and anything else that is directly linked to combat activities. It had its own administrations, such as the operational administration, based on commanders' decisions. It was in charge of issuing directives, orders and information. The next sector is the training sector. Actually, sorry, it is an administration, administration for training, in charge of training soldiers and officers in the VRS. The third segment, albeit it is not an administration, are the heads of combat arms directly linked to the Main Staff. The chief of the Main Staff is also deputy commander because, in this seven-box structure, it was supposed to be the first among equals and that is why that person also is tasked with being deputy commander, because he was also in charge of combat activities on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to explain who Major General Miletic is and what his responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Miletic was the chief of the operations administration in the staff sector. In terms of function, he was my deputy. That is to say, deputy of the Chief of Staff, which does not automatically mean that he was the deputy in the -- my capacity of deputy commander. The task of his administration was to translate information into orders, as ordered by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, to help us understand the role of each sector, can you tell us what would be the responsibilities of your sector in the case of a hypothetical military operation to take control of a town called A?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The task of my sector, or, rather, my task, that I am supposed to implement through the three administrations, the training administration, the combat arms administration, and the operations administration, was as follows: First of all, assessing the situation, having in mind the enemy, the possibility of our own armed forces to act in a particular area. Also, I had to submit a proposal to the commander, in terms of how the operation should be carried out. If the commander accepts it, he can accept it partially or as a whole. Once the commander has said, "I have decided," irrespective of what my proposal was, these administrations, and primarily Miletic's administration, is in charge of issuing documents, be it directives, orders, information, or anything of the sort. Later on, they would also be in charge of analysis, anything envisaged by the commander is something the operations administration is supposed to translate into combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, between your sector the staff sector and the other components of the Main Staff, we see a green line which, according to the legend, indicates coordination. Can you briefly tell us how this worked in practice, this coordination function?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In practice, coordination mainly took place at the Main Staff meetings. General Mladic had, under his direct command, my sector, the staff sector, then the sector for morale, religious and legal affairs, headed by General Gvero, also the logistics sector providing materiel support headed by General Djukic. Next, the sector for the organisation, mobilisation and manning levels, headed by Petar Skrbic whereas initially it had been General Grubor. The next sector is the intelligence and security administration headed by General Tolimir. He also had two administrations directly linked to him because they could not be placed within any of the sectors. The administrations being the one for planning and finance, headed by General Stevo Tomic, and the administration for the air force and anti-aircraft defence headed by Jovo Maric. Later, it was Colonel Radoslav Pantic, since Maric was killed at some point. In any case, it was towards the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, can we return to some of the sectors so that I can you some specific questions. With respect to the sector on moral guidance, religious and legal affairs, what would be the responsibility of this sector with respect to this hypothetical operation to take control of Town A?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That sector, first of all, had to ascertain the level of morale in our ranks, i.e. whether the armed force is capable to fight, whether it is willing to fight or reluctant to fight. Secondly, he had to tour the units, which were supposed to implement the task, in order to explain the soldiers, and I always told General Gvero that he had to hold meetings to tell soldiers about the importance of particular tasks, so as to encourage those with low morale, in order to have it raised to an appropriate level. In addition to working on their morale, his sector was also in charge of legal affairs pertaining to the VRS. In other words, they monitored the work of military courts, they initiated or launched certain court proceedings, unless it was done by the military prosecutor's office, and they also controlled and analysed their work. The third task they had was -- were religious affairs. He was supposed to be in contact with the various religious communities in the territory of Republika Srpska in order to meet their requests or to place requests before them. For example, to make it possible for the soldiers to freely express their religious denomination, et cetera. So in general terms, cooperating with the various religious communities in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: With respect to the logistics sector, what would its responsibility be in terms of this hypothetical operation, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first task of the sector would be to tell us what we have at our disposal. How many pieces of weapons, how much ammunition, how much food, fuel, based on the calculations by the Main Staff. They were also supposed to ensure that sufficient qualities [as interpreted] are available. The sector was not tasked with distributing it to units individually because it was done by the staff sector. It was in charge of distributing the so-called strategic materiel such as weapons, ammunition, fuel, food, clothing and footwear. That was within the competence of the staff sector. Every soldier, every day, irrespective of whether it is peacetime or wartime, has to be clothed and I delegated that responsibility to the logistics sector, whereas I retained the right of the staff sector to be in charge of distributing the three main assets: Weapons, ammunition and fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now if we go to the bottom of the diagram, we see 21 boxes, six of them containing the name of corps, one the name the air force and air defence and the remainder different units whose name is indicated in the individual box. I want to draw your attention to some of those boxes, which have more relevance to this particular case, and ask you to explain their primary responsibilities. Can I first direct your attention to the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment? Can you tell us what its primary responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The very name of the regiment speaks to its tasks. It is a protecting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Motorised Protection Regiment providing protection to the Main Staff or individuals from the Main Staff temporarily detached from Crna Rijeka. It was headed by Milomir Savcic. He was promoted from Captain First Class to Colonel. They had units trained to defend the Main Staff and the main command post and they also used it frequently as the Main Staff's reserve to intervene at such front lines where there was need to do so. In any case, they were used to reinforce other corps. We rarely used it to provide security at the command location. We mainly used it to assist other units, depending on where the situation was at its worst at a particular point in time at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Under that box, we can see Military Police Battalion. Can I ask you to describe what its responsibilities or function was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The MP Battalion was part of the Motorised Protection Regiment. The Intervention Unit was a unit supposed to keep internal order and discipline in other units. In addition to the MP Battalion there was the Protection Regiment had two motorised battalions which were supposed to go in combat. They were also in charge of regular policing that the military police usually does, including providing security for the prominent officers of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly repeat which particular officers he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The interpreters are asking to you repeat the names of the officers that you mentioned. They didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment, as we can see here is Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic. The MP Battalion commander is Major Zoran Malinic. He was there throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now could I draw your attention to the 10th Sabotage Detachment? Could I ask you to describe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm wondering whether -- what the interpreters asked, whether that is -- I got the impression that they were asking for the prominent officers of the army which were included in the security system. Now, the answer seems to be about who was the commander of that 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. Witness, did you -- when you said that the military police provided security for the prominent officers of the army, did you mention any prominent officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not. That is why I think the interpreters intervened. For example I did not mention the MP Battalion commander's name but I did say that his military police was to provide security for the prominent figures in the VRS who were mainly from the Main Staff because the corps had their own military police in charge of it. Do you want me to specify the names of the people that the military police was supposed to provide security for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need to do that unless Mr. Groome would ask you for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, did General Mladic have the authority to give a direct order to anyone in the army?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can find it under item "command" in the military lexicon. A commander has the right to issue orders to anyone in the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Mladic abided by that rule. For example, if he wanted to issue an order to someone in the brigade, he went through the corps commander. Karadzic, as the Supreme Commander, by the same token, had the right to order -- issue orders two levels down, say to a corps commander, but he was duty-bound to inform General Mladic of it. When such a person received an order from the Supreme Commander, at the earliest opportunity, he had to notify General Mladic of having received such orders from the Supreme Commander. In this case, General Mladic needed not to go through me as his deputy to issue a task to, say, another sector. For example, to Skrbic, who was in charge of organisation, mobilisation and manning levels. He could do it directly because Skrbic was his direct subordinate. He was his assistant for mobilisation. By the same token General Djukic was also his assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, could I return to my earlier question about the 10th Sabotage Detachment? Can you tell us what its area of responsibility and function was?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I realised there was a mistake. The 2nd Sabotage Detachment --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The 10th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in -- directly linked to Colonel Salapura in the intelligence administration. The intelligence administration was supposed to collect data on the enemy, neighbours, et cetera. They engaged in the so-called forceful acquiring of information. When that was necessary, they would engage the sabotage detachment. Forceful acquiring of information, in other words, means provoking a conflict with the enemy in a particular area to observe its reaction, and based on the intensity of fire or the width of the front line and its depth, the sabotage and reconnaissance personnel could assess the enemy's strength, size, power, et cetera. One can acquire information in two ways: By observation, following documents and so on, or by forceful reconnaissance. Each subordinate unit, such as the corps and brigades, had their respective reconnaissance units for that. The sabotage detachment was used by Colonel Salapura for the very thing, to acquire forcefully information on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now my final question on this diagram is -- the Chamber has heard evidence about municipal Crisis Staffs. Did municipal Crisis Staff have any role to play in the command structure of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. During the first meeting of the Main Staff, I think the third conclusion that was reached was: To remove the power from the Crisis Staffs to command the armed forces, including the 85 to 90.000 men I mentioned, who were armed at the time. That intention of ours was not implemented quickly, though, because the brigades, and later on when the VRS was established, had strong links with their respective municipalities in terms of food supply, clothes and even fuel supply. Those people who provided financial assistance believed that they had the right to command the brigade that they supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you but I'm conscious of the time and my only query was whether or not they had a role to play in the command structure. Could I now turn your attention to your office and General Mladic's office? Can you describe that office and where you sat in respect to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, while the witness is changing his glasses, could I tender 65 ter 26016 into evidence as a public exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26016 receives number P2212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2212 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So, General, can you describe where your desk was in relation to General Mladic's?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The very first evening when we gathered, General Mladic, inter alia, said the following: I probably won't quote him precisely. But it was to the effect that General Milovanovic was supposed to be his deputy. He said everything I know he needs to know too. Alluding to the importance of that with his assistants, saying that they ought to keep me informed as well as General Mladic unless it is done during a common meeting. He said that the room where we assembled, which was at the entrance to the northern building in the first office on the right-hand side, he said that it was to be our joint office, that is to say his and mine. He said that there may be opportunities when he would with be at the front lines and I would be there, and vice versa, so he was trying to save space. We had a single desk, which faced my seat, that is to say the drawers were on my side, whereas General Mladic always sat on the opposite side. If one of us was away from the Main Staff, General Miletic came to be there instead of the person who was absent. That is how we rotated throughout the war. Next to the office was my resting room, so from the office one could enter the room where I rested, whereas General Mladic had his resting premises about a kilometre away. Under the regulations, the commander and his deputy could not spend the night in each other's proximity so as to avoid having both of them killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 26005 be brought to our screens? After the Chamber has had an opportunity to see the title of the document, could I ask the usher to move to the second page of the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General Milovanovic, when you see the document on the screen, can you familiarise yourself with it? I'm not interested in the substance of the document. What I'm interested in is for you to review the list of telephone extensions belonging to members of the Main Staff. And my question is simply whether these extension numbers are accurate, to the best of your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is dated the 28th of September, 1995, which is when I was on the western front, be it in Drvar, Mrkonjic Grad or Banja Luka. I can't tell you precisely. But I don't see any phone numbers here. You may have mentioned another page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You have to go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe I see them on the page in B/C/S on the screen if I'm not mistaken. It's just below the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see it. Okay. I see them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So it records your telephone number as extension 155. Do you recall that as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And with respect to the other extension numbers of the other people there, do you recall those extensions as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say whether they are correct or not. I even forgot my own extension, and in one of my testimonies, I was reminded by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did General Mladic ever use your telephone extension with respect to either making phone calls or receiving phone calls?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The extension 155 was the extension of the Main Staff. It is next to my name here because I was the chief of the Main Staff. That is to say the most senior person. It was in my and General Mladic's office. Whenever the phone went off, if General Mladic was there, we did not have an assistant or secretary to answer the call, and it was always done by the most senior person in the office. In this case, the person being General Mladic. So in other words, yes, he did use it. I also had a line installed in my bedroom, as well as in the operations centre, where there were between 12 and 15 people on a daily basis making up the team that was on duty. It was also installed in the building where General Mladic was during the night. It was also installed in the subterranean command location in the operations room. So on a daily basis, there could have been some 30 people who passed by that phone. To conclude, General Mladic regularly used this extension whenever we were in the office together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: To clarify, you've now mentioned a physical location, several physical locations of phones. Am I correct in understanding your evidence that if someone rang 155, the appropriate phone would ring, whether you were in your office or your bedroom or some of these other locations that you've described?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We had an automatic switchboard. If somebody wanted to talk to me personally, then the switchboard operator would first dial the extension in my office. If I wasn't there, especially during the night, he would then dial the number in my bedroom. If I wasn't there either, then he would dial the extension number in the operations centre. Those people, the duty officers, always knew where to find me. If somebody wanted to talk to General Mladic, the procedure would be the same. The only thing that they would skip would be my bedroom. I don't know how the switchboard operators did that. In any case, it never happened that all the telephones that responded to the number 155 rang at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just before the break could I tender this Exhibit 65 ter 26005 as a public exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 26005 receives number P2213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Milovanovic, you may follow the usher. We'll take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness will be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, I'd like to return for a moment to that period of time when the VRS was being established and ask you: What role did the existing JNA rules and doctrines play in the establishment of VRS rules and doctrines?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since most of us had been trained in the JNA, we were familiar with those rules and regulations, and that's why it was decided that we should continue applying them in the Army of Republika Srpska. Obviously, to a lesser extent, in accordance with the size of the army, the territory where it operated, the conduct of the enemy towards us, and the material or financial circumstances of the state, and of its army. We adopted all the rules and regulations of the JNA and adapted them to our needs, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, you've made a reference to the two roles that you held. One was Chief of Staff to General Mladic, and also deputy commander. Could I ask you to spend a few moments describing the different responsibilities that each of those titles held?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As Chief of Staff, I managed the staff sector, first and foremost, and then the staff as a whole. This means that I organised its work, submitting reports to the commander about the work of the staff, and as the deputy commander, I stood in for the commander when he was not in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Or if I was authorised by him to be in charge of a sector, either in the western front or the eastern front, in the Podrinje area, in Herzegovina, wherever he sent me, I would have the right to make fully legitimate decisions instead of the commander. Standing in for the commander could last for up to 30 days, according to JNA rules. And if the commander didn't return within 30 days, either somebody else would be appointed, or I would be appointed as fully fledged commander, and then my replacement would be appointed. Luckily enough no such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: In Mladic's absence, when you're serving in the capacity of deputy commander, did you have the authority to issue an order to anyone in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But I had to inform General Mladic about everything that I undertook, that I ordered, or any similar thing that happened during his absence. And then he would either approve my move or he would evoke [as interpreted] my decision, but in most cases he approved my decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, when General Mladic is present, and you're serving as his Chief of Staff, do you have the authority to issue an order to anyone in the VRS without informing him or without his consent?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if General Mladic left the country on a particular day, and you became deputy commander, would you have changed or withdrawn orders that Mladic had issued just prior to leaving the country?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not even in a condition that something happened to Mladic. For as long as his decision was in effect, it would have been fully implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: General, one of the terms used by military organisations is "command and control." Can I ask you to explain to the Chamber, in theoretical terms, what the understanding of this concept was to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Command and control is a common term in the definition for managing military in wartime and in peacetime. But let me talk about wartime. Warfare is something that politicians do. It was the Presidency of the Serbian Republic until the command was set up. And then it was the same people when the Supreme Command was set up, it was the Supreme Command who was in charge of war. So the Supreme Command issues a decision to start a war or to launch wartime activities, to determine war objectives and targets, and to declare the war over. However, the command and control functions exist in the army as well, especially when it comes to strategic and operative commands. It is there that the Main Staff and the corps commands, to a certain extent, run the war policy, they collect information on the enemy, they propose to the Supreme Command as to how the military as a whole should be used, how its separate parts should be used. It is very difficult to separate the two functions, the control and the command functions. I take the liberty to say that command means to implement control, or it is a direct element of the control function. And now on to the command function. Command is centralised, first and foremost, and it goes top to bottom, from the Supreme Command, across the Main Staff, corps commands, brigade commands, battalion commands, to the commands of companies, squads. Persons in charge are commanders in units higher than the battalion and komandirs for units that are smaller than a company, including a company. The command function has to be and it was in our military centralised, it was continuous, and every activity had to finish with an analysis exercise. In the meantime, between the analysis and the previously issued order - which means that issuing order is also an element of the command function - there is or -- the supervision or control of how the order is implemented. Some militaries in -- of the world have the so-called control organs in their staffs. We didn't have that. We only introduced that towards the end of the war, after the Dayton Accords were signed, we set up a group that controlled combat readiness. During the war, we did that through our command system. If an operation involved several corps, somebody from the Main Staff would be assigned, it would be either the commander or his assistant, who would be in charge of that operation that involved two or more corps. The commander would authorise us to be in full command in such sectors. It was usually one of the two of us, either General Mladic or I, that would be sent to such a sector. If war operations involving two or more corps were taking place in two separate areas, then one of us would be sent to one place, and the other to the other. Or the commander, in order to ensure the continuity of the work of the Main Staff could assign one of his other assistants, apart from me, to be in charge or rather to command such a combat operations. I believe that that happened only once during the war, General Gvero was assigned to be in command of the operation Pancir that involved the Sarajevo-Romanija and Drina Corps who were both engaged on the front line facing Olovo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, earlier today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could I take the parties back to page 44, line 6, where it reads: And then he would either approve my move or he would evoke my decision. I understood that logically to be revoke my decision, but since evoke is an existing word as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If the Chamber likes I could clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we -- could do it right away.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter confirms that the word should have been "revoke."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it has been confirmed by the interpreters that we have to understand the answer as revoke. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, earlier today, you described that one of the first tasks that General Mladic assigned to you was to establish communications, and that you did this on the 12th of May. Can I ask you to tell us, what is the relationship between effective communications and effective command and control?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Orders and information that were issued by the superior bodies to the inferior units are conveyed in several ways. The first way is using telephone. Obviously, it has to be a protected telephone line during the war. The second way was to be -- was to send coded texts. The third way was to use radio communication system. We used this very little between the strategic and operational level. It is normally used on a tactical level. And the fourth way was using couriers, i.e. couriers would be physically carrying mail. When I spoke about establishing communication with corps command using a button, the push of a button, I wanted to emphasise the speed of conveying a message from superior command to all the subordinated -- subordinate units and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Clarification of a matter which appears in the transcript as between brackets with a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I clarify something to make sure that the record accurately records your evidence. When you said radio communications were used, in what types of operations were radio -- was radio communication typically used?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Radio communication means were most commonly used in tactical conditions, i.e. in actions, I can't say operations. However, in the course of fighting that involved brigades and battalions. That would be the tactical level because those units were on a tactical level and they were the ones who most commonly used radio communication means. Using the command code for the secret command of units. So this was a coded message. They would say one thing when sending a message, and the receiver would understand the message although the words that were used were completely different. So there was a coded message. For example, the message could be: Launch an attack 555. The subordinated unit would understand that 555 is actually the code for launch an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, between the time that you established communications on the 12th of May, 1995, until the very end of the conflict, at the end of -- I'm sorry, 1992, 12th of May, 1992, until the very end of the conflict at the end of 1995, was there ever a time that communication systems failed?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it happened on the 29th of August, 1995, when NATO started bombarding the Army of Republika Srpska. It lasted for 17 days. On the first day, 13 Tomahawk projectiles were launched, all of them at the same time, and they hit all of our 13 communications hubs. For two hours after that, we did -- our system was not operational, all of our systems were down. That was the only interruption. In the course of the war, there were small interruptions here or there in a smaller area but they were never total interruptions in the communication system.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without going into detail, how many levels of backup were there in the event the primary communication system failed? How many independent systems were there?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to call them communication system sets. We inherited our communication systems from the 2nd Military District, i.e. the command of the 2nd Military District. We also inherited the communication system of the republican staff of Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was headquartered in Pale. And we also had a communication set of the brigade of the Supreme Command, which had withdrawn from Sarajevo back to Serbia, i.e. the personnel and the vehicles withdrew and what remained behind were the communication system. That's how we ended up with one set always operational, the second at the ready, and a third set was usually out for repairs in one of our factories, either Cajevic or Kosmos in Banja Luka. The fourth set, the courier communications is what I didn't mention because the only thing that we had as parts of that system were couriers and their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do I understand your evidence correctly that between the 12th of May, 1992, and the end of the war in 1995, there was only one complete interruption of the communication systems for two hours and then there were some minor interruptions that were restricted to a particular geographic area? Do I understand your evidence correctly in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, General, I want to return to the concept of command and control, and would I be correct in saying that the conduct of regular meetings was an important feature of how General Mladic exercised his command and control over VRS troops?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will ask you detailed questions about these meetings. To assist the Chamber, can I ask you first to list all of the regular meetings and then all of the ad hoc meetings and then I will ask specific questions about each one, including who was present and what was the typical agenda. My first question is: Did Mladic have a regular daily meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When he was in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did Mladic hold a weekly reporting meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic had regular meetings, every day, every morning. Those meetings started around 7.00 in the morning. If needed, those meetings were also organised in the afternoon, if anything had happened during the day that required such a meeting to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'll ask you some very specific questions about this meeting. First, who were the regular attendees at this regular daily meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The commander and all of his assistants. It also happened that deputies of the commanders' assistants were present. For example, General Miletic would sometimes attend with me. Colonel Kovacevic was sometimes with General Djukic. Later on, Colonel Milanovic would also attend. Savo Sokanovic sometimes attended together with Gvero. In other words, us assistants were allowed to bring on our assistants or deputies, but most often it was only the commander and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And to be clear, when you use the phrase "assistant," you're referring to the assistant commanders in charge of the different sectors and components of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the deputies of the chiefs of various sectors. There were no sector commanders. There were sector chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned that during certain periods, it was held more than once a day. Can I ask you to summarise which periods of the conflict this was and at what time of the day would such meeting typically be held?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those evening meetings would take place if something changed on the front lines. For example, if we had lost some territory or we -- if we had suffered major losses. Or if in the meantime the Supreme Command had requested something from us or ordered us to do something, it was then that the commander would invite us to an evening meeting in order to decide as to how to react, whether to try and return the lost territory, how to carry out and implement the Supreme Commander's order, i.e. how to remedy any situation that may have occurred during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one matter in relation to the regular morning meetings. Mr. Milovanovic, you told us who were the regular participants, and I think the last question of Mr. Groome was not properly understood and answered. You said the assistants were present, and the question of Mr. Groome was were the assistant commanders in the Main Staff present during these morning meetings. The assistant commanders meaning the chiefs of administrations. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did understand it, but I'm waiting for your permission to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When I finished my question, you were allowed to speak. Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way I understood your question, or Mr. Groome's question, was that Mr. Groome misspoke when he said "commanders." It was not commanders but chiefs of sectors. There was just one commander in the staff, and that was General Mladic. All the others, including me, we were all chiefs. So when I said "assistants," Mr. Groome interpreted that as commanders' assistants but those were the assistants of the chiefs. In the army, we speak about the person's titles starting or ending with a K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that but exactly that is the misunderstanding. I understood the question of Mr. Groome to be: Are these the assistant commanders who are the chiefs of sectors in the Main Staff? Are they called assistant commanders of the commander of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Each of the sector chiefs is also the assistant commander for that sector. Just as I was also the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is now well understood. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I'm looking at the clock. It would be time to adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That would be a suitable place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Milovanovic, we will adjourn for the day. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone or communicate in whatever other way about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or whether that's testimony still to be given. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 18th of September, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
